# SkillComposer: Learning to Evolve Agent Skills for Specification and Generalization

###### Abstract

Agent skills, which consist of reusable strategies that guide agent
reasoning and action, have shown strong potential for improving model
capability at inference time. However, current skill construction
methods treat the problem as one-shot extraction, overlooking a
fundamental tension: a skill tailored to the specific task fails to
transfer, while the abstracted skill often provides insufficient
guidance. We attribute this fragility to the absence of explicit
mechanisms for skill specification and generalization. To address this
gap, we introduce SkillComposer, a framework that decomposes skill
construction into three learnable operations: create, improve, and
merge. Trained via systematic rejection sampling recipe, SkillComposer
enables language models to self-evolve skills at inference time and
supports three deployment modes: offline for building generalized
libraries, online for task-specific refinement, and hybrid for combining
both. Comprehensive experiments on $`\tau^{2}`$-Bench, LiveCodeBench v6,
and AppWorld show that SkillComposer consistently outperforms baselines.
Our SkillComposer-4B improves a 27B executor by up to +4.5 on agent
tasks and +3.4 on code tasks, while generalizing across domains and task
types unseen during training. Analysis reveals that merge and improve
address orthogonal quality dimensions and that skill composition is a
transferable meta-ability, providing a practical recipe for
skill-augmented inference.

## 1 Introduction

Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable progress
across a wide range of tasks, yet they still struggle with novel
scenarios that demand structured problem-solving strategies [Xu and Yan
(2026)](#bib.bib5). To bridge this gap, recent work has introduced agent
skills: reusable natural-language instructions, each comprising a name,
a trigger condition, and a procedural body, that encode domain-specific
procedures in a modular format [Anthropic (2025)](#bib.bib3); [Wang et
al. (2025)](#bib.bib19). By loading relevant skills into the context,
models can leverage accumulated experience without parameter updates,
offering a lightweight and interpretable mechanism for capability
enhancement [Liang et al. (2026)](#bib.bib20).

![Refer to caption](2606.06079v1/intro_fig.png)

Figure 1: Three deployment modes of SkillComposer. Offline builds a
generalized skill library via creation and merging; Online creates and
iteratively refines skills per task; Hybrid initializes from an offline
library and specializes via online evolution.

Despite their promise, current skill-based approaches face several
fundamental limitations: they rely on high-quality human-written
skills [Li and others (2026)](#bib.bib11) or on extracting procedural
knowledge from successful trajectories [Fang et al. (2026)](#bib.bib14),
both of which are costly and difficult to scale. When models generate
skills autonomously, the results often yield limited or even negative
performance gains, as the models lack mechanisms for quality control,
refinement, and abstraction [Ni et al. (2026)](#bib.bib18); [Ling et al.
(2026)](#bib.bib21). More critically, effective skills require both
generalization (abstracting across similar tasks to produce transferable
strategies) and specification (tailoring skills to particular task
patterns), yet existing methods provide no systematic way to achieve
either. A skill that is too specific fails to transfer to other relevant
tasks, while one that is too general provides insufficient guidance for
other particular tasks [Ling et al. (2026)](#bib.bib21); [agentskills
(2025)](#bib.bib4).

In this work, we observe that skill construction can be decomposed into
three learnable abilities: (1) Skill Create extracts reusable procedural
knowledge from raw execution trajectories, (2) Skill Merge drives
generalization by consolidating semantically similar skill pairs into
broader, more transferable ones, and (3) Skill Improve drives
specification by refining a skill to better capture task-specific
patterns based on new execution experience. Together, these operations
define a complete lifecycle for skill evolution: from initial
extraction, through cross-task abstraction to iterative refinement. We
propose SkillComposer, which enables language models to self-evolve its
skills at inference time without ground-truth supervision. Moreover, we
use delta pass rate guided rejection sampling to synthesize supervised
fine-tuning data to further enhance these three abilities.

Building on these abilities, SkillComposer supports three modes of
operation that address different practical scenarios
(Figure [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ SkillComposer: Learning to Evolve Agent Skills for Specification and Generalization")).
In Offline mode, the model builds a general-purpose skill library from a
training set via iterative creation and merging, and retrieves relevant
skills for new tasks at inference time. In Online mode, the model starts
with an empty library and iteratively creates and refines skills on the
fly, driving specification in real time. This mode requires no prior
data and is applicable to open-ended or streaming scenarios. Hybrid mode
combines both by initializing with a generalized offline library and
then specializing it through online evolution, balancing broad coverage
with task-specific adaptation. We evaluate SkillComposer on code
generation (LiveCodeBench v6) and agent tasks ($`\tau^{2}`$-Bench,
AppWorld), demonstrating consistent improvements across models and
domains. Our contributions are as follows:

- •
  We identify specification and generalization as two orthogonal
  dimensions of skill quality, and decomposing skill construction into
  creating, improving, and merging provides an explicit mechanism for
  this trade-off.
- •
  We propose SkillComposer, a rejection-sampling-based framework that
  teaches language models to compose, refine, and abstract skills,
  supporting offline, online, and hybrid deployment modes.
- •
  Comprehensive experiments across multiple benchmarks, model scales,
  and both in-domain and out-of-distribution settings demonstrate the
  effectiveness and generalization of SkillComposer. Analysis further
  reveals that Skill Merge and Improve address complementary quality
  dimensions and that skill composition transfers across task types,
  providing a practical recipe for skill-augmented inference.

## 2 Related Work

Agent skills and skill libraries. Agent skills have recently emerged as
a practical abstraction for extending LLM agents at inference time.
Unlike a single tool call, a skill package reusable procedural
knowledge, trigger conditions, and sometimes executable resources that
can be loaded on demand [Anthropic (2025)](#bib.bib3); [Xu and Yan
(2026)](#bib.bib5). Recent work has therefore studied how to build,
organize, and reuse skill libraries. SkillX constructs a plug-and-play
skill knowledge base by distilling trajectories into hierarchical skills
and refining them with execution feedback [Wang et al.
(2026)](#bib.bib1). SkillRL distills past experience into a hierarchical
SkillBank and lets the skill library co-evolve with an agent policy
during reinforcement learning [Xia et al. (2026)](#bib.bib6).
Complementary work upgrades textual skills into executable program
functions that intervene in the agent loop [Liu et al.
(2026a)](#bib.bib7). These works show that skills can serve as compact
experience carriers for LLM agents. However, they mainly treat skills as
external artifacts to be collected, retrieved, or optimized, while the
ability to construct high-quality skills remains dependent on human
authoring, successful trajectories, or external optimization loops.

![Refer to caption](2606.06079v1/main_fig.png)

Figure 2: The lifecycle of a skill under SkillComposer. A skill is first
created from a raw execution trajectory (creation). Multiple
semantically similar while task-specific skills are then consolidated
via Skill Merge to form broader, more transferable skills (specification
$`\rightarrow`$ generalization). When applied to a new task, a
generalized skill is iteratively refined via Skill Improve to better fit
the target task (generalization $`\rightarrow`$ specification). The
resulting specialized skill is finally consumed by the skill executor to
guide inference.

Skill evolution and quality control. Closest to our work are recent
methods that move from static skill reuse to automatic skill evolution.
EvoSkill discovers and edits skills through iterative failure analysis
and validation [Alzubi et al. (2026)](#bib.bib8); CoEvoSkills couples a
skill generator with a surrogate verifier to build multi-file skill
packages without ground-truth test content [Zhang et al.
(2026)](#bib.bib9); and SkillClaw aggregates cross-user interaction
traces to collectively refine a shared skill repository [Ma et al.
(2026)](#bib.bib10). Meanwhile, benchmark studies reveal that skill
benefits are fragile: curated skills can substantially improve agents,
but self-generated skills may provide no average gain [Li and others
(2026)](#bib.bib11), and skill utility degrades under realistic
retrieval and adaptation settings [Liu et al. (2026b)](#bib.bib12).
These findings suggest that the core bottleneck is not merely having
more skills, but constructing skills with explicit quality control,
task-level specification, and cross-task generalization. Different from
prior work, SkillComposer decomposes skill construction into three
trainable abilities–create, improve, and merge–and learns them through
rejection-sampled supervision filtered by delta pass rate. In this way,
skill evolution becomes an intrinsic capability of the language model
itself: Skill Improve drives specification, Skill Merge drives
generalization, and the resulting model can self-evolve skill libraries
in offline, online, and hybrid settings.

## 3 Methodology

In this section, we dive into the framework of SkillComposer. We first
formalize three core skill operations
(§[3.2](#S3.SS2 "3.2 Skill Operations Formulation ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ SkillComposer: Learning to Evolve Agent Skills for Specification and Generalization")),
then describe how they compose into three inference-time application
scenarios
(§[3.3](#S3.SS3 "3.3 Inference-Time Skill Evolution ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ SkillComposer: Learning to Evolve Agent Skills for Specification and Generalization")),
and finally introduce a rejection-sampling-based training procedure that
strengthens these operations
(§[3.4](#S3.SS4 "3.4 Training via Rejection Sampling ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ SkillComposer: Learning to Evolve Agent Skills for Specification and Generalization")).
Figure [2](#S2.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 2 Related Work ‣ SkillComposer: Learning to Evolve Agent Skills for Specification and Generalization")
provides an overview of the lifecycle of a skill under our proposed
SkillComposer.

### 3.1 Preliminary

We begin by formalizing the concept of agent skills. In the most general
form, agent skills comprise a markdown-style document SKILL.md along
with optional auxiliary files such as references, scripts, and
assets [Anthropic (2025)](#bib.bib3). In this work, we focus on the main
body of agent skills, where each skill $`s`$ is defined as a tuple of
three components: a name $`n`$, a description $`d`$, and a body $`b`$.
The name serves as an identifier, the description specifies the trigger
condition under which the skill should be activated, and the body
encodes the procedural strategy to be followed.

### 3.2 Skill Operations Formulation

Maintaining a high-quality skill library requires addressing three
fundamental challenges: i) how to extract a reusable skill from a raw
trajectory produced without any skill guidance, ii) how to prevent the
unbounded growth of a skill library while promoting generalization, and
iii) how to refine an existing skill based on new execution experience.
We address these challenges by introducing three composable operations:
create, merge, and improve.

Skill Create. When the agent solves a task without leveraging any prior
skill, the resulting trajectory contains implicit procedural knowledge
that can benefit future tasks with a similar structure. Skill Create
distills such a trajectory into a reusable skill:

|     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- |
|     |

       ``` math
       s={\rm SkillComposer_{create}}(x,{\rm LLM}(x))
       ```                                             |     |

Skill Merge. As skills accumulate, the library risks unbounded growth
and over-specification, where many narrowly-scoped skills overlap in
functionality. To mitigate this, Skill Merge consolidates two
semantically similar skills, $`s_{1}`$ and $`s_{2}`$, into a single,
more general one:

|     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- |
|     |

       ``` math
       s={\rm SkillComposer_{merge}}(s_{1},s_{2})
       ```                                         |     |

Specifically, to measure the semantical similarity of two skills, we
introduce a multi-view similarity mechanism where we compute similarity
across every dimension for each skill pair:

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
{\rm sim}(s_{1},s_{2})=\frac{1}{3}\sum_{I\in\{n,d,b\}}{\rm sim}(I_{1},I_{2})
``` |  | (1) |

Only pairs with similarity larger than a threshold $`\delta`$ will be
selected to conduct Skill Merge.

Skill Improve. When the agent solves a task under the guidance of an
existing skill $`s_{\rm o}`$, the resulting trajectory may reveal new
patterns or refinements that the original skill does not capture. Skill
Improve incorporates these insights to produce a more effective skill:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
s={\rm SkillComposer_{improve}}(x,s_{\rm o},{\rm LLM}(x,s_{\rm o}))
``` |  |

### 3.3 Inference-Time Skill Evolution

The three operations can be chained in different orders depending on
whether a pre-existing task set is available and whether task-specific
refinement is desired at inference time. We organize these compositions
into three deployment modes.
Algorithm [1](#alg1 "Algorithm 1 ‣ 3.4 Training via Rejection Sampling ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ SkillComposer: Learning to Evolve Agent Skills for Specification and Generalization")
also unifies the three modes into a single procedure:

Offline. The most straightforward way to leverage skills at inference
time is to pre-build a skill library from a given task set. In offline
mode, we first generate raw trajectories for all tasks and apply Skill
Create to extract one skill per trajectory. We then compute pairwise
similarities using
Equation [1](#S3.E1 "In 3.2 Skill Operations Formulation ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ SkillComposer: Learning to Evolve Agent Skills for Specification and Generalization")
and iteratively merge the most similar pairs until no pair exceeds
$`\delta`$. The resulting library captures generalized procedural
knowledge. At inference time, we retrieve the top-$`k`$ skills for each
target task and employ a self-select mechanism that allows the executor
to choose the most appropriate skill, or abstain if none is relevant.

Online. In scenarios where no pre-existing task set is available, we
operate in online mode. For each incoming task, the agent generates a
raw trajectory and applies Skill Create to initialize a skill. The skill
is then iteratively refined: at each iteration, the agent re-executes
the task under the current skill’s guidance, and Skill Improve updates
the skill based on the new trajectory. This process repeats for a fixed
number of iterations $`T`$, progressively driving specification.

Hybrid. The hybrid mode combines the strengths of both approaches. It
initializes with an offline-constructed skill library, then applies
online evolution on top. For each new task, we retrieve and self-select
a relevant skill from the library, then refine it through iterative
improvement. This enables the model to start from a generalized
foundation and progressively specialize toward the target task.

### 3.4 Training via Rejection Sampling

While any language model can perform the three operations zero-shot, the
output quality varies considerably. We strengthen them via supervised
fine-tuning on rejection-sampled data [Yuan et al. (2023)](#bib.bib24),
using a unified quality signal: delta pass rate, the performance change
caused by a candidate skill. A training example is accepted only when
the candidate improves the executor’s pass@$`k`$ relative to the
appropriate baseline by at least a threshold $`\epsilon`$.

Concretely, we generate $`n`$ raw trajectories per task and apply the
base model to produce candidate skills. For create, we compare the
executor’s pass@$`1`$ with and without the candidate skill on the source
task and retain the example if the improvement exceeds
$`\epsilon_{\rm c}`$:

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\Delta_{\text{create}}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\text{pass@}1(\text{LLM}(x,s))`$ |  |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\quad-\text{pass@}1(\text{LLM}(x))\geq\epsilon_{\rm c}`$ |  | (2) |

For merge and improve, the criterion generalizes to multiple evaluation
tasks. Merge assesses the consolidated skill $`s`$ against the two
original skills $`s_{1},s_{2}`$ on their respective source tasks
$`x_{1},x_{2}`$:

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\Delta_{\text{merge}}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^{2}\big[\text{pass@}1(\text{LLM}(x_{i},s))`$ |  |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\quad-\text{pass@}1(\text{LLM}(x_{i},s_{i}))\big]\geq\epsilon_{\rm m}`$ |  | (3) |

Improve evaluates the refined skill against the original skill
$`s_{\rm o}`$ on both the source task $`x`$ (from which $`s_{\rm o}`$
was derived) and a target task $`x^{\prime}`$:

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\Delta_{\text{improve}}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{x_{i}\in\{x,x^{\prime}\}}\big[\text{pass@}1(\text{LLM}(x_{i},s))`$ |  |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\quad-\text{pass@}1(\text{LLM}(x_{i},s_{\rm o}))\big]\geq\epsilon_{\rm i}`$ |  | (4) |

For improve, we include both cross-task ($`x^{\prime}\neq x`$) and
same-task ($`x^{\prime}=x`$) pairs, so the training signal captures both
specification and generalization. Detailed algorithms for all three
procedures are provided in
Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B Rejection Sampling Procedures ‣ SkillComposer: Learning to Evolve Agent Skills for Specification and Generalization").

0:  Task set $`\mathcal{X}`$, skill executor LLM, mode $`\in`$ {offline,
online, hybrid}, max iterations $`T`$, skill library
$`\mathcal{L}\leftarrow\emptyset`$

0:  Evolved skill library $`\mathcal{L}`$

1:  Stage 1: Skill Library Initialization

2:  if mode $`\in`$ {offline, hybrid} then

3:   for each task $`x\in\mathcal{X}`$ do

4:    $`\tau\leftarrow\text{LLM}(x)`$ $`\triangleright`$ Raw trajectory

5:    $`s\leftarrow\text{SkillComposer}_{\text{create}}(x,\tau)`$

6:    $`\mathcal{L}\leftarrow\mathcal{L}\cup\{s\}`$

7:   end for

8:   repeat

9:
   $`(s_{i},s_{j})\leftarrow\text{RetrieveSimilarPair}(\mathcal{L},\delta)`$

10:    $`s\leftarrow\text{SkillComposer}_{\text{merge}}(s_{i},s_{j})`$

11:
   $`\mathcal{L}\leftarrow(\mathcal{L}\setminus\{s_{i},s_{j}\})\cup\{s\}`$

12:   until no similar pairs remain

13:  end if

14:  Stage 2: Skill Evolution

15:  for each target task $`x^{\prime}`$ do

16:   if mode = offline then

17:
   $`s\leftarrow\text{SelfSelect}(\text{Retrieve}(\mathcal{L},x^{\prime},k))`$

18:    $`\tau\leftarrow\text{LLM}(x^{\prime},s)`$

19:   else

20:    if mode = online then

21:     $`\tau\leftarrow\text{LLM}(x^{\prime})`$

22:
    $`s\leftarrow\text{SkillComposer}_{\text{create}}(x^{\prime},\tau)`$

23:    else if mode = hybrid then

24:
    $`s\leftarrow\text{SelfSelect}(\text{Retrieve}(\mathcal{L},x^{\prime},k))`$

25:    end if

26:    for $`t=1`$ to $`T`$ do

27:     $`\tau\leftarrow\text{LLM}(x^{\prime},s)`$

28:
    $`s\leftarrow\text{SkillComposer}_{\text{improve}}(x^{\prime},s,\tau)`$

29:    end for

30:   end if

31:   $`\mathcal{L}\leftarrow\mathcal{L}\cup\{s\}`$

32:  end for

## 4 Experiments

### 4.1 Experimental Settings

#### Training and Evaluation

For coding task, we use OpenCodeReasoning [Ahmad et al.
(2025)](#bib.bib17) for both rejection sampling and building the initial
skill library. For rejection sampling of the agent task, we follow
AutoForge ([Cai et al., 2025](#bib.bib2)) to synthesize datasets similar
to the Retail domain in $`\tau^{2}`$-Bench. In summary, we synthesize
around 7,000 supervised fine-tuning data points. We further train
Qwen3.5-4B [Team (2026)](#bib.bib22) with LlamaFactory, and run skill
executor and SkillComposer using vllm. We extend more implementation
details in
Appendix [A](#A1 "Appendix A Implementation Details ‣ SkillComposer: Learning to Evolve Agent Skills for Specification and Generalization").

#### Benchmarks

We evaluate SkillComposer on three benchmarks spanning agent and code
tasks. (1) $`\tau^{2}`$-Bench [Barres et al. (2025)](#bib.bib15) is a
multi-turn agent benchmark that simulates realistic customer service
interactions across three domains: Retail, Airline, and Telecom. Each
domain requires the agent to follow domain-specific policies and execute
tool calls to resolve user requests. Since the training data only
consists of the Retail domain, evaluation on Airline and Telecom can be
regarded as a cross-domain scenario. (2) LiveCodeBench v6 [Jain et al.
(2024)](#bib.bib16) is a contamination-free code generation benchmark
comprising problems of varying difficulty (Easy, Medium, Hard) sourced
from recent programming contests. (3) AppWorld [Trivedi et al.
(2024)](#bib.bib13) is an interactive agent benchmark that requires
autonomous app usage through API calls across diverse everyday
applications. We use AppWorld as an out-of-distribution evaluation to
assess cross-task generalization, as it is entirely unseen during
training.

#### Effectiveness of SkillComposer.

On the 4B executor, SkillComposer consistently outperforms both
baselines and its untrained counterparts across all modes. The hybrid
mode achieves the best $`\tau^{2}`$-Bench score (85.7, $`+`$6.2 over No
Skill), while the online mode leads on LiveCodeBench (59.1, $`+`$2.5).
MemP degrades LiveCodeBench performance to 47.4, well below the No Skill
baseline of 56.6, underscoring the risk of uncontrolled skill
extraction. In contrast, SkillComposer online improves over its
untrained counterpart by 2.0 points on $`\tau^{2}`$-Bench and 2.4 points
on LiveCodeBench, confirming that rejection-sampling-based training
yields meaningful quality gains. We provide detailed performance curves
across iterations in
Appendix [C](#A3 "Appendix C Performance by Iteration ‣ SkillComposer: Learning to Evolve Agent Skills for Specification and Generalization")
(Figure [5](#A3.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ Appendix C Performance by Iteration ‣ SkillComposer: Learning to Evolve Agent Skills for Specification and Generalization")).

Moreover, we further provide inference efficiency comparison across the
base model and our trained SkillComposer-4B. As shown in
table [6](#A4.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ Appendix D Inference Efficiency across Iterations ‣ SkillComposer: Learning to Evolve Agent Skills for Specification and Generalization"),
as skills evolve, the average token consumption of both methods
decreases while the average performance keep increasing, which indicates
the steady performance and efficiency of our methods. Notably, except
for the performance superiority, our trained SkillComposer-4B also
consistently show better efficiency.

#### Comparison across modes.

Online and hybrid consistently outperform offline, indicating that
iterative skill refinement at inference time provides substantial gains
beyond static retrieval. Hybrid achieves the strongest
$`\tau^{2}`$-Bench results by combining a generalized library with
online specialization. Notably, the performance gains of offline and
hybrid modes are more pronounced on $`\tau^{2}`$-Bench than on
LiveCodeBench. We attribute this to the offline library construction:
the $`\tau^{2}`$-Bench library is built from its in-distribution
training set, while the code library draws from only 500 randomly
sampled OpenCoderReasoning instances, which offers limited coverage of
LiveCodeBench’s task distribution.

In contrast, the online mode, which requires no pre-built library and
instead refines skills per task, excels on LiveCodeBench, where
task-specific specification is most beneficial. Furthermore, on
Hard-level code problems, hybrid consistently outperforms online (31.3
vs. 29.3 on 4B; 67.2 vs. 66.8 on 27B), suggesting that an initial skill
library serves as valuable prior experience that particularly benefits
the executor on more challenging tasks where structured guidance is most
needed. However, on the Simple and Medium-Level problems, hybrid lags
behind the online setting, which indicates that unnecessary skills might
mislead the language models when facing simpler tasks.

### 4.3 Cross-Model Generalization

Since all training data is collected with Qwen3.5-4B as the skill
executor, the 27B results directly evaluate cross-model transfer. As
shown in
Table [1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 4.2 Main Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ SkillComposer: Learning to Evolve Agent Skills for Specification and Generalization"),
SkillComposer generalizes effectively across model scales:
SkillComposer-4B-online achieves 88.0 on $`\tau^{2}`$-Bench ($`+`$4.5
over No Skill) and 83.1 on LiveCodeBench ($`+`$3.4), while the hybrid
mode reaches 67.2 on Hard-level code problems. These results confirm
that skills composed by a smaller model remain effective when consumed
by a substantially larger executor, suggesting that skill quality is
largely decoupled from the composer’s capacity.

### 4.4 Cross-Domain Generalization

Our $`\tau^{2}`$-Bench training data is sourced exclusively from the
Retail domain, making Airline and Telecom results a direct test of
cross-domain generalization. On the 4B executor, SkillComposer-4B-hybrid
achieves 82.5 on Airline ($`+`$13.7 over No Skill) and 95.6 on Telecom
($`+`$2.5). On the 27B executor, SkillComposer-4B-online reaches 83.5 on
Airline ($`+`$6.0) and 98.8 on Telecom ($`+`$4.4). The Airline gains
suggest that skills learned from Retail, which shares structural
similarities as a customer-service domain, transfer effectively to
related but unseen domains. This indicates that SkillComposer acquires
generalizable composition abilities rather than domain-specific
patterns.

## 5 Ablation and Analysis

We now investigate the mechanisms behind SkillComposer’s gains. We first
ablate the individual skill operations to verify that merge and improve
serve complementary roles
(§[5.1](#S5.SS1 "5.1 Ablation on Skill Operations ‣ 5 Ablation and Analysis ‣ SkillComposer: Learning to Evolve Agent Skills for Specification and Generalization")).
We then ask whether the learned composition ability is tied to the
training domain or transfers across task types
(§[5.2](#S5.SS2 "5.2 Transferability of Skill Composition ‣ 5 Ablation and Analysis ‣ SkillComposer: Learning to Evolve Agent Skills for Specification and Generalization")),
whether it generalizes to entirely unseen benchmarks
(§[5.3](#S5.SS3 "5.3 Cross-Task Generalization ‣ 5 Ablation and Analysis ‣ SkillComposer: Learning to Evolve Agent Skills for Specification and Generalization")),
and whether iterative skill evolution offers genuine advantages over
brute-force repeated sampling
(§[5.4](#S5.SS4 "5.4 Iterative Evolution vs. Repeated Sampling ‣ 5 Ablation and Analysis ‣ SkillComposer: Learning to Evolve Agent Skills for Specification and Generalization")).

### 5.1 Ablation on Skill Operations

We ablate the skill operations used during offline library construction
to isolate each operation’s contribution.
Table [2](#S5.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 5.1 Ablation on Skill Operations ‣ 5 Ablation and Analysis ‣ SkillComposer: Learning to Evolve Agent Skills for Specification and Generalization")
reports offline-mode results with Qwen3.5-4B as the skill executor.

| Skill Operations     | $`\tau^{2}`$-Bench | LiveCodeBench v6 |
|----------------------|--------------------|------------------|
| Create               | 73.8               | 58.5             |
| Create/Improve       | 75.6               | 57.3             |
| Create/Merge         | 77.5               | 59.0             |
| Create/Merge/Improve | 76.9               | 57.9             |

Table 2: Ablation on skill operations used during offline library
construction (Qwen3.5-4B executor). Skill Merge provides the largest
gain by promoting generalization, while Skill Improve is less beneficial
in the offline setting, where transferability is prioritized.

Skill Merge is the most impactful operation: adding it to Skill Create
yields $`+`$3.7 on $`\tau^{2}`$-Bench and $`+`$0.5 on LiveCodeBench.
This aligns with our framework’s design, as offline libraries prioritize
generalized skills, and Skill Merge is precisely the operation that
drives generalization. To visualize this effect,
Figure [3](#S5.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 5.1 Ablation on Skill Operations ‣ 5 Ablation and Analysis ‣ SkillComposer: Learning to Evolve Agent Skills for Specification and Generalization")
shows t-SNE embeddings of the Retail skill library before and after
merging. After Skill Merge, the skill distribution becomes notably
sparser, confirming that merge effectively consolidates redundant skills
into fewer, more general ones. Adding Skill Improve alone to Create
provides moderate gains on $`\tau^{2}`$-Bench ($`+`$1.8) but slightly
hurts LiveCodeBench ($`-`$1.2), suggesting that specification can reduce
transferability for unseen tasks. Combining all three operations
performs slightly below Skill Create/Merge, indicating that
indiscriminate specification during offline construction partially
counteracts the generalization benefit of Skill Merge. These results
reinforce that Skill Improve is better suited for online and hybrid
settings, where skills are refined toward specific target tasks.

Figure 3: t-SNE visualization of the Retail skill library before (left)
and after (right) Skill Merge. Merging consolidates semantically similar
skills, producing a sparser and more general library with reduced
redundancy.

### 5.2 Transferability of Skill Composition

We investigate whether the skill composition ability generalizes across
task types or remains specific to the training scenario. We train
SkillComposer with agent-only, code-only, and mixed (agent & code)
rejection sampling data, evaluating all variants on LiveCodeBench v6 in
online mode with Qwen3.5-27B as the skill executor
(Table [3](#S5.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 5.2 Transferability of Skill Composition ‣ 5 Ablation and Analysis ‣ SkillComposer: Learning to Evolve Agent Skills for Specification and Generalization")).

| SkillComposer             | Easy  | Medium | Hard | Overall |
|---------------------------|-------|--------|------|---------|
| Qwen3.5-4B                | 100.0 | 91.9   | 64.5 | 81.4    |
|             +agent        | 100.0 | 93.5   | 66.8 | 82.9    |
|             +code         | 99.5  | 95.8   | 68.0 | 84.0    |
|             +agent & code | 100.0 | 94.2   | 66.8 | 83.1    |

Table 3: Transferability of skill composition across task types,
evaluated on LiveCodeBench v6 (online mode, Qwen3.5-27B executor).
Agent-only training still improves code performance, confirming that
skill composition is a general-purpose ability.

Training with agent-only data improves overall performance from 81.4 to
82.9 ($`+`$1.5), despite never encountering code tasks during training.
This confirms that skill composition is a general-purpose ability:
structuring procedural knowledge and iterative refinement transfer
across task types. Code-only training yields the strongest results
(84.0, $`+`$2.6) due to direct domain alignment, while the mixed setting
used in practice achieves 83.1, offering a balanced trade-off.

### 5.3 Cross-Task Generalization

To further evaluate whether SkillComposer generalizes to entirely unseen
agent tasks, we test the online mode on AppWorld [Trivedi et al.
(2024)](#bib.bib13), a benchmark not used during training or rejection
sampling. We compare the vanilla model (No Skill), the untrained
Qwen3.5-4B composer, and SkillComposer-4B, all using Qwen3.5-4B as the
skill executor. Results are shown in
Table [4](#S5.T4 "Table 4 ‣ 5.3 Cross-Task Generalization ‣ 5 Ablation and Analysis ‣ SkillComposer: Learning to Evolve Agent Skills for Specification and Generalization").

SkillComposer-4B achieves the best performance on both metrics,
improving accuracy to 57.7 ($`+`$2.5 over Vanilla) while maintaining a
high pass rate of 88.3. Notably, the untrained composer improves
accuracy (57.1) but degrades pass rate from 88.1 to 86.0, indicating
that naively generated skills can introduce errors that reduce task
completion reliability. In contrast, SkillComposer improves both metrics
simultaneously, confirming that rejection-sampling-based training
produces skills that enhance correctness without sacrificing robustness.
This result demonstrates that the skill composition ability learned from
$`\tau^{2}`$-Bench transfers effectively to a structurally different
agent benchmark.

| Method    | Vanilla | Qwen3.5-4B | SkillComposer-4B |
|-----------|---------|------------|------------------|
| Accuracy  | 55.2    | 57.1       | 57.7             |
| Pass Rate | 88.1    | 86.0       | 88.3             |

Table 4: Cross-task generalization on AppWorld (online mode, Qwen3.5-4B
executor). SkillComposer improves both accuracy and pass rate, while the
untrained composer degrades pass rate.

### 5.4 Iterative Evolution vs. Repeated Sampling

A natural question is whether iterative skill evolution offers
advantages beyond simply sampling more attempts. To answer this, we
compare two strategies under the same inference budget of $`k`$ rounds:
i) vanilla pass@$`k`$, which independently samples $`k`$ solutions
without any skill and selects the best one, and ii) SkillComposer online
evolution, which creates a skill from the first trajectory and
iteratively improves it across $`k`$ rounds.

As shown in
Figure [4](#S5.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 5.4 Iterative Evolution vs. Repeated Sampling ‣ 5 Ablation and Analysis ‣ SkillComposer: Learning to Evolve Agent Skills for Specification and Generalization"),
both strategies start from the same baseline at $`k{=}1`$, but
SkillComposer consistently outperforms vanilla pass@$`k`$ as the number
of rounds increases. On the 4B executor, SkillComposer reaches 73.71 at
$`k{=}5`$ compared to 69.71 for vanilla pass@$`k`$, a gain of 4.0
points. On the 27B executor, the gap persists at 91.43 vs. 88.57
($`+`$2.86). Notably, the performance gap widens with each additional
round, indicating that iterative skill refinement compounds its
advantage over independent sampling. This demonstrates that structured
skill evolution is a more effective use of additional inference budget
than brute-force repeated sampling.

Figure 4: Pass@$`k`$ vs. SkillComposer online evolution over $`k`$
rounds on LiveCodeBench v6. Both strategies share the same starting
point at $`k{=}1`$. Iterative skill refinement consistently outperforms
independent repeated sampling, with the gap widening as $`k`$ increases.

## 6 Conclusion

We presented SkillComposer, a framework that decomposes skill
construction into three learnable operations: create, improve, and
merge. By training these operations via rejection sampling filtered by
delta pass rate, SkillComposer enables language models to self-evolve
skill libraries at inference time without ground-truth supervision. The
framework supports three complementary modes: offline for building
generalized libraries, online for task-specific refinement, and hybrid
for combining both. Experiments on $`\tau^{2}`$-Bench, LiveCodeBench v6,
and AppWorld demonstrate that SkillComposer consistently outperforms
baselines and generalizes across model scales, domains, and task types.
Our analysis further reveals that merge drives generalization while
improve drives specification, and that skill composition is a
transferable ability that benefits from but does not require in-domain
training data.

## Limitations

The rejection sampling procedure requires multiple inference passes per
task to compute delta pass@$`k`$, making training data collection
computationally expensive. Additionally, our experiments are conducted
with a limited number of model families (Qwen3.5-4B and Qwen3.5-27B);
evaluating SkillComposer across a broader range of architectures and
scales would strengthen the generality of our findings.

## Appendix A Implementation Details

In this paper, we use Qwen3-Embedding-8B [Zhang et al.
(2025)](#bib.bib23) as the embedding model to calculate the similarity.
We list the global hyperparameter settings across all tasks below:

| Parameter                                              | Value |
|--------------------------------------------------------|-------|
| similarity threshold $`\delta`$                        | 0.8   |
| delta pass rate for Skill Create $`\epsilon_{\rm c}`$  | 0.4   |
| delta pass rate for Skill Merge $`\epsilon_{\rm m}`$   | 0.4   |
| delta pass rate for Skill Improve $`\epsilon_{\rm i}`$ | 0.4   |

Table 5: Hyperparameters details for rejection sampling.

### A.1 Code

#### Rejection Sampling

For rejection sampling, we use 8,000 data points sampled from
OpenCodeReasoning, and run 5 separate runs for each data point.

#### Skill Library Building

For the initial skill library building of offline and hybrid modes, we
incorporate 500 randomly sampled data points from the OpenCodeReasoning
dataset.

### A.2 Agent

#### Skill Library Building

For the initial skill library building of offline and hybrid modes, we
use the training split of $`\tau^{2}`$-Bench.

### A.3 Evaluation Details

For agent tasks, we conduct 4 separate runs across all methods and
settings. For code tasks, we conduct 5 separate runs across all methods
and settings. Finally, we report the average score of the best iteration
across all runs for each setting. Moreover, during the skill library
building of the evaluation process, we use the same similarity threshold
$`\delta`$ as rejection sampling.

### A.4 Training Details

For supervised fine-tuning, we trained Qwen3.5-4B with LlamaFactory. We
list the detailed hyperparameters below:

|---------------------------|--------|
| Parameter                 | Value  |
| Learning Rate             | 1e-6   |
| Train Batch Size          | 64     |

## Appendix B Rejection Sampling Procedures

We provide detailed pseudo-code for the three rejection sampling
procedures introduced in
§[3.4](#S3.SS4 "3.4 Training via Rejection Sampling ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ SkillComposer: Learning to Evolve Agent Skills for Specification and Generalization").

0:  Task set $`\mathcal{X}`$, skill executor LLM, base composer
$`\mathcal{C}`$, samples $`n`$, threshold $`\epsilon_{\rm c}`$

0:  Training set $`\mathcal{D}_{\text{create}}`$

1:  $`\mathcal{D}_{\text{create}}\leftarrow\emptyset`$

2:  for each task $`x\in\mathcal{X}`$ do

3:   $`p_{\text{base}}\leftarrow\text{pass@}1(\text{LLM}(x),n)`$

4:   $`\tau\leftarrow`$ sample one trajectory from LLM$`(x)`$

5:   $`s\leftarrow\mathcal{C}_{\text{create}}(x,\tau)`$

6:   $`p_{\text{skill}}\leftarrow\text{pass@}1(\text{LLM}(x,s),n)`$

7:   if $`p_{\text{skill}}-p_{\text{base}}\geq\epsilon_{\rm c}`$ then

8:
   $`\mathcal{D}_{\text{create}}\leftarrow\mathcal{D}_{\text{create}}\cup\{(x,\tau)\rightarrow s\}`$

9:   end if

10:  end for

Algorithm 2 Rejection Sampling for Skill Create

0:  Skill-task pairs $`\{(s_{i},x_{i})\}`$, skill executor LLM, base
composer $`\mathcal{C}`$, samples $`n`$, threshold $`\epsilon_{\rm m}`$

0:  Training set $`\mathcal{D}_{\text{merge}}`$

1:  $`\mathcal{D}_{\text{merge}}\leftarrow\emptyset`$

2:  Compute pairwise similarity among all skills

3:  for each similar pair $`(s_{1},x_{1})`$, $`(s_{2},x_{2})`$ do

4:   $`s\leftarrow\mathcal{C}_{\text{merge}}(s_{1},s_{2})`$

5:
  $`\Delta\leftarrow\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^{2}[\text{pass@}1(\text{LLM}(x_{i},s),n)-\text{pass@}1(\text{LLM}(x_{i},s_{i}),n)]`$

6:   if $`\Delta\geq\epsilon_{\rm m}`$ then

7:
   $`\mathcal{D}_{\text{merge}}\leftarrow\mathcal{D}_{\text{merge}}\cup\{(s_{1},s_{2})\rightarrow s\}`$

8:   end if

9:  end for

Algorithm 3 Rejection Sampling for Skill Merge

0:  Skill-task pairs $`\{(s_{i},x_{i})\}`$, skill executor LLM, base
composer $`\mathcal{C}`$, samples $`n`$, threshold $`\epsilon_{\rm i}`$

0:  Training set $`\mathcal{D}_{\text{improve}}`$

1:  $`\mathcal{D}_{\text{improve}}\leftarrow\emptyset`$

2:  Compute skill-task similarity matrix

3:  for each selected pair $`(s_{\rm o},x^{\prime})`$ with original task
$`x`$ do

4:   $`\tau^{\prime}\leftarrow`$ sample one trajectory from
LLM$`(x^{\prime},s_{\rm o})`$

5:
  $`s\leftarrow\mathcal{C}_{\text{improve}}(x^{\prime},s_{\rm o},\tau^{\prime})`$

6:
  $`\Delta\leftarrow\frac{1}{2}\sum_{x_{i}\in\{x,x^{\prime}\}}[\text{pass@}1(\text{LLM}(x_{i},s),n)-\text{pass@}1(\text{LLM}(x_{i},s_{\rm o}),n)]`$

7:   if $`\Delta\geq\epsilon_{\rm i}`$ then

8:
   $`\mathcal{D}_{\text{improve}}\leftarrow\mathcal{D}_{\text{improve}}\cup\{(x^{\prime},s_{\rm o},\tau^{\prime})\rightarrow s\}`$

9:   end if

10:  end for

Algorithm 4 Rejection Sampling for Skill Improve
